127.title: Confirmation
127.hook: the bishop anoints the forehead with perfumed oil: be sealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit
127.howItsDone: In the Latin Church most Catholics are confirmed as young people by the bishop, who anoints their foreheads with chrism; Eastern Catholics and the Orthodox receive chrismation as babies right after baptism.

segments.voice: Yesterday, baptism: water three times, in three names. Your line was your first birthday. Did you find the date, or who was there? Day one hundred twenty-seven.

If you've ever been to a Catholic confirmation, you might remember the smell before anything else. The church is full, teenagers in their best clothes lined up in the aisle, families craning to see. One by one they step up to the bishop, often with a sponsor's hand on their shoulder. The bishop dips his thumb in oil and traces a cross on each forehead. And as he gets closer, the whole front of the church smells faintly sweet, like a perfume counter. That smell has a name. Today's word: chrism.
screen: `TEENAGERS IN THE AISLE.` → `A THUMB, A CROSS, A FOREHEAD.` → `THE SMELL OF PERFUME.`

segments.voice: Chrism is olive oil mixed with balsam, a fragrant resin. Once a year, usually in Holy Week, each bishop consecrates it at a special Mass, and it's sent out to every parish. The word comes from the Greek chrisma, an anointing. And it's the same root as Christ, Christos, which means the anointed one. In the Bible, kings, priests and prophets were anointed to mark them for a task. In the book of Acts, the people of Samaria hear the Gospel and are baptized. The apostles in Jerusalem send Peter and John, and in the Douay-Rheims, "they laid their hands upon them, and they received the Holy Ghost." Confirmation, Catholics say, continues that moment. As the bishop anoints, he says, in the English form, be sealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit. Sealed, like wax pressed with a signet ring: a mark that says this belongs to someone. The Catholic Church teaches confirmation completes baptism and strengthens a person to live the faith in public. Tradition names seven gifts of the Spirit, drawn from Isaiah: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear of the Lord. The timing differs. Eastern churches anoint babies right after baptism; they call it chrismation. In the Latin Church, it usually comes years later, or for adults at Easter. And then there's the name. Many people being confirmed choose a saint's name. It's a custom, not a rule, and in some places it's fading, often because nobody explained it. In the Bible, a new name marks a new task: Abram becomes Abraham, Simon becomes Peter. The point isn't a cool middle name. It's choosing a friend among the saints, someone whose life you'd like to grow into and whose prayers you can ask for. Some keep their baptismal name instead, a sign that confirmation completes baptism.
screen: `OLIVE OIL AND BALSAM.` · `CHRISMA: THE SAME ROOT AS CHRIST.` · `HANDS LAID ON IN SAMARIA.` · `A SAINT'S NAME: A FRIEND FOR THE ROAD.` · then, large: `SEALED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for one gift. Settle, and breathe. Listen to the seven again, slowly: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, fear of the Lord. Fortitude is courage that lasts. Counsel is knowing what to do. Piety is a warm love for God. Which one do you need this week? Pick one. If you pray, you can ask the Holy Spirit for it by name. If you don't, just hold it as a hope, the thing you'd want to be marked with. The bell holds the time.
Chrism. Olive oil and balsam, blessed by the bishop, from the same Greek root as Christ. The oil of confirmation. Today's word.
Your line: sealed. Today, when you need your one gift, touch your forehead for a second and remember you're marked, not alone. Day one hundred twenty-seven.

128.title: The Eucharist
128.hook: the source and summit of the Christian life (CCC 1324)
128.howItsDone: Catholics receive the Eucharist at Mass, which the Church asks them to attend each Sunday, after a first Communion in childhood, and fast for an hour beforehand.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chrism, the sweet oil of confirmation. Your line was sealed. Which gift of the Spirit did you ask for? Day one hundred twenty-eight.

A river starts somewhere small: a spring in the hills, a trickle coming up out of the ground. Every boat, mill and town downstream depends on that spring. A mountain works the other way round. Its paths start in different valleys, on different sides, and every one of them is headed for the same place: the top. The Catholic Church borrows those two pictures, source and summit, for one sacrament, and hangs the whole Christian life between them. Today, the Eucharist.
screen: `A SPRING IN THE HILLS.` → `A PATH TO THE TOP.` → `SOURCE AND SUMMIT.`

segments.voice: Eucharist is a Greek word, eucharistia, and it means thanksgiving. At the Last Supper, the Gospels say, Jesus took bread and gave thanks, and the sacrament takes its name from that thanks. We've already walked through the Mass piece by piece, the consecration, and Justin's Sunday. Today's idea is bigger: where the Eucharist sits in everything else. The Second Vatican Council called it the source and summit of the whole Christian life, and the Catechism repeats it in paragraph 1324. Source: the other sacraments, the Church's work, a Catholic's prayer, all flow out of it, like a river from its spring. Summit: they all lead back to it, like paths up a mountain. Baptism brings you to the table. Confirmation strengthens you to live what you receive there. Confession clears the way back to it. Priests are ordained above all to celebrate it. Catholics believe that in the Eucharist Jesus himself is truly present, body and blood, soul and divinity, which is why they call it the sacrament of sacraments. Paul puts another side of it in one line. In the Douay-Rheims: "For we, being many, are one bread, one body, all that partake of one bread." The table doesn't only feed each person; it makes them one body. Day one hundred and fourteen set out how other Christians understand the meal. All of them keep the table.
screen: `EUCHARISTIA: THANKSGIVING.` · `SOURCE: EVERYTHING FLOWS FROM IT.` · `SUMMIT: EVERYTHING LEADS TO IT.` · `ONE BREAD, ONE BODY.` · then, large: `WE, BEING MANY, ARE ONE BREAD, ONE BODY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with two words, source and summit. Settle, and breathe. On the in-breath, think source: what is the spring your day comes out of? Rest, love, a person, God. On the out-breath, think summit: what is your day really climbing toward? Don't answer quickly. Just let the two words go back and forth with your breathing. If you pray, you can give thanks, which is what the word Eucharist means. The bell holds the time.
The Eucharist. From the Greek for thanksgiving. For Catholics, the source that everything flows from, and the summit everything climbs toward. Today's word.
Your line: everything flows from the table. Today, thank one person out loud for something you usually take for granted. That's the word Eucharist, in miniature. Day one hundred twenty-eight.

129.title: Reconciliation: can I come back?
129.hook: the fear of mortal sin keeps people away for years; the sacrament of return is a door, not a wall
129.howItsDone: Catholics who have been away can return to Mass at any time; those aware of serious sin go to confession before receiving Communion. Many parishes offer confession on Saturday afternoons, and priests are used to hearing 'it's been a long time, and I don't remember how.'

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Eucharist, source and summit. Your line was everything flows from the table. Did you thank someone out loud? Day one hundred twenty-nine.

A text at one in the morning, typed and deleted three times, to the one friend who still goes to Mass. Is it true I can't come back until I confess? I haven't been in six years. Am I in mortal sin? Do I have to fix everything first? The friend isn't sure either. So the question goes back in the drawer, and another year goes by. A lot of people carry some version of that text. It deserves a straight answer, and a kind one. Today: reconciliation.
screen: `A TEXT AT 1 A.M.` → `AM I IN MORTAL SIN?` → `A STRAIGHT ANSWER, AND A KIND ONE.`

segments.voice: First, what the Church actually teaches, without softening it. The Catechism says that skipping Sunday Mass on purpose, with no serious reason, is a grave matter. Being sick, caring for someone, or being somewhere with no Mass within reach is not a sin at all. And for any sin to be mortal, three things must all be true at once: grave matter, full knowledge, and deliberate consent. We'll go deeper on that later in the year. Then the Catechism adds a line worth remembering: we can judge that an act is wrong, but the judgment of persons belongs to God alone. Nobody gets to pronounce a verdict on your soul from the parking lot. Not even you. Second, what to actually do. Mass is open; you can go this Sunday. If there may be serious sin, Catholics wait on Communion and go to confession first. That isn't a fee at the door. It is the door. The sacrament's name says so. Reconciliation, from the Latin reconciliare: to bring together again. Jesus tells of a son who wastes everything and walks home with a speech rehearsed. In the Douay-Rheims: "when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and was moved with compassion, and running to him fell upon his neck, and kissed him." The father runs before the speech is done. Third, when the fear won't let go. Some people confess, hear the words of forgiveness, and still can't believe it. They check and recheck every thought for sin. Catholic spiritual writers have an old name for this: scrupulosity. The Church meets it gently. A steady confessor helps, and so can a good counselor; it isn't a lack of faith. Fourth, the feeling afterward. Some walk out in tears of relief. Some feel awkward, or nothing at all. Catholics believe the forgiveness is just as real either way.
screen: `WHAT MAKES A SIN MORTAL: ALL THREE.` · `MASS IS OPEN. CONFESSION IS THE DOOR.` · `SCRUPULOSITY: WHEN FEAR WON'T LET GO.` · `FORGIVEN, FELT OR NOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be met on the road. Settle, and breathe. Picture a long road home, and yourself on it, going over what you'd say. Now picture someone far off at the end of it, who has already seen you, and is already running. Don't finish the speech. Let yourself be met halfway. If there's something you've been carrying, let it come along as it is. If you pray, you can hand it to God in a word. The bell holds the time.
Reconciliation. From the Latin for bringing back together. The sacrament of return, where Catholics confess to a priest and hear that they're forgiven: a door, not a wall. Today's word.
Your line: there's always a way back. Today, take one small step toward someone you're at odds with. A message, a smile, a hello. Day one hundred twenty-nine.

130.title: Anointing of the sick
130.hook: not only for the dying; oil for anyone seriously ill or old (CCC 1514)
130.howItsDone: A Catholic who is seriously ill, frail with age or facing major surgery can ask a priest for the anointing, at home, in hospital, or at a parish Mass for the sick; it can be received more than once.

segments.voice: Yesterday, reconciliation, the sacrament of return. Your line was there's always a way back. Did you take one small step toward someone? Day one hundred thirty.

A hospital room, late afternoon. A woman in her seventies is going in for heart surgery tomorrow. Her daughter has called the parish, and a priest comes in with a small oil stock in his pocket, the size of a lipstick. The daughter looks nervous. Isn't this, she whispers, what they do when someone's dying? The priest smiles. It's a common mix-up. Her mother isn't dying. She's sick, and scared, and that's exactly who this is for. Today, the anointing of the sick.
screen: `A HOSPITAL ROOM, THE DAY BEFORE.` → `ISN'T THIS FOR THE DYING?` → `IT'S FOR THE SICK.`

segments.voice: For a long time this sacrament was called extreme unction, the last anointing, and in practice it was often saved for the very end. So some people still think of it that way: the priest arrives, and it's time to say goodbye. After the Second Vatican Council, the Church changed the name and the emphasis. It's the anointing of the sick, and the Catechism says it's for anyone who begins to be in danger of death from sickness or old age. Not dying: beginning to be in danger. Before major surgery. When a chronic illness gets worse. When age makes a person frail. And it can be received again, if the illness returns or worsens. The roots are in the letter of James. In the Douay-Rheims: "Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord." James goes on to say the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up. The priest lays his hands on the person's head in silence, then anoints the forehead and the hands with the oil of the sick, blessed by the bishop. Only a priest can give it. What do Catholics believe it does? Strength, peace and courage to face the illness, union with Christ's own suffering, forgiveness, and sometimes, if God wills, bodily healing. It doesn't replace doctors. Catholics go to both. When someone is truly near death, the priest may also hear their confession and give Communion, called viaticum, food for the journey. Those together are what people mean by last rites.
screen: `NOT ONLY THE LAST ANOINTING.` · `IS ANY MAN SICK AMONG YOU?` · `HANDS, OIL, FOREHEAD AND PALMS.` · `STRENGTH, PEACE, AND SOMETIMES HEALING.` · then, large: `THE SICK ARE NOT FORGOTTEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone who is ill. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who is sick or in the hospital, or very old and frail. See their face. Picture the room they're in. If you know what they're afraid of, hold that too. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't pray, simply keep them company in your mind for the length of the bell. The bell holds the time.
Extreme unction. The old name for anointing of the sick, oil on the forehead and hands, for anyone seriously ill or old, not only the dying. Today's word.
Your line: the sick are not forgotten. Today, send one message, or make one call, to someone who is ill. Ask how they are, and then listen. Day one hundred thirty.

131.title: Holy orders
131.hook: deacons, priests and bishops ordained by the laying on of hands
131.howItsDone: Catholic deacons, priests and bishops are ordained by a bishop, usually in a cathedral, through the silent laying on of hands and a prayer of consecration, after years of formation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the anointing of the sick, extreme unction. Your line was the sick are not forgotten. Who did you call or keep in mind? Day one hundred thirty-one.

At one point in an ordination Mass, a young man in a white robe walks to the front of a packed cathedral and lies down. Flat on the floor, face down, arms at his sides. The congregation kneels and sings a long list of saints' names, asking each one to pray for him. It goes on for minutes. Somewhere in the pews, his mother may be in tears. It's a startling thing to see in a church: a man giving his whole body to the ground before he's given a job. Today's word: ordination.
screen: `A YOUNG MAN LIES FACE DOWN.` → `A LONG LIST OF SAINTS.` → `HIS WHOLE BODY TO THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: Ordination comes from the Latin ordo, an order or rank, the word Romans used for the groups that made up their society. The sacrament is called holy orders, plural, because there are three: deacons, priests and bishops. The names are Greek. Deacon is diakonos, a servant, someone who waits on tables. Priest comes, through old English, from presbyteros, an elder. And bishop comes from episkopos, an overseer. Each one is a kind of serving. The sign is very old: hands laid on the head in silence. In the book of Acts, seven men are chosen to care for widows, whom Catholic tradition counts as the first deacons, and in the Douay-Rheims, "they praying, imposed hands upon them." The letters to Timothy also recall a gift that came through the laying on of hands. At an ordination today, the bishop lays his hands on the candidate's head without a word, then prays the prayer of consecration. At a priest's ordination, every priest present comes up and lays on hands too. Catholics believe this sacrament, like baptism, marks a person for good. Priests celebrate the Eucharist and hear confessions; deacons baptize, preach, witness marriages and serve the poor; bishops lead a diocese and ordain others. In the Latin Church, priests and bishops are normally celibate, while permanent deacons can be married, and Eastern Catholic churches have married priests. The Church ordains only men, and teaches that it has no authority to ordain women as priests; some Catholics hope that will change. Other Christians understand ministry differently: the Orthodox keep the same three orders; Anglicans keep bishops, priests and deacons too; other Protestant churches ordain ministers but generally don't count ordination as a sacrament.
screen: `ORDO: AN ORDER, A RANK.` · `SERVANT, ELDER, OVERSEER.` · `HANDS LAID ON IN SILENCE.` · `MARKED FOR GOOD, TO SERVE.` · then, large: `CALLED TO SERVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a short litany. At an ordination, the church sings name after name over the man on the floor, asking each to pray for him. Settle, and breathe. Let names come, one for each breath. If you pray and know some saints, use theirs: Mary, Joseph, Peter, and answer each one quietly, pray for us. If you don't, use the names of people who served you well: a teacher, a nurse, a grandmother. One name, one breath, and a moment of thanks. The bell holds the time.
Ordination. From the Latin for an order. Deacons, priests and bishops, made by the laying on of hands to serve. Today's word.
Your line: called to serve. Today, thank one person who serves you, a priest, a pastor, a nurse, a bus driver, out loud and by name. Day one hundred thirty-one.

132.title: Matrimony
132.hook: in the Latin Church the couple are the ministers; they give the sacrament to each other
132.howItsDone: Catholics usually marry at a Mass or wedding service in church, exchanging vows before a priest or deacon and two witnesses, after a period of marriage preparation with the parish.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ordination: deacons, priests and bishops, and hands laid on in silence. Your line was called to serve. Who did you thank by name? Day one hundred thirty-two.

Here's a trivia question that surprises most Catholics. At a Catholic wedding, who gives the sacrament? Most people would say the priest. He's the one in vestments, standing in the middle, asking the questions. But in the Latin Church, the answer is: the bride and the groom. The priest or deacon is there as the Church's witness. The two people holding hands are the ones doing it. They give the sacrament to each other. Today, the last of the seven sacraments: matrimony.
screen: `WHO GIVES THE SACRAMENT?` → `NOT THE PRIEST.` → `THE BRIDE AND THE GROOM.`

segments.voice: Matrimony comes from Latin, matrimonium, built on mater, mother. It's an old Roman word, looking ahead to family. In the Latin Church, the heart of the sacrament is consent: two people freely saying yes to each other, for life, in front of witnesses. That's why the couple are the ministers. Their promise is the sign. The priest or deacon asks, and blesses, and receives the vows for the Church. In the Eastern churches it's understood differently: the priest's blessing is essential, and the couple are crowned, as a king and queen of a new little kingdom. Jesus speaks about marriage in Matthew's Gospel, going back to Genesis. In the Douay-Rheims: "Therefore now they are not two, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let no man put asunder." Paul, writing to the Ephesians about husbands and wives, says in the Douay-Rheims, "This is a great sacrament; but I speak in Christ and in the church." The Latin Bible used the word sacramentum there, and it helped shape how the Church came to see marriage: a human love that shows God's own faithful love. Catholics understand it as lifelong, faithful, and open to children. So the Church doesn't recognize divorce as ending a valid marriage, though it can declare, after careful review, that a marriage was never valid to begin with. Other Christians see marriage in different ways: many Protestant churches treat it as holy but not a sacrament, and the Orthodox, in some cases, allow a second marriage. That completes the seven: three to bring you in, two to heal, two to serve.
screen: `MATRIMONIUM, FROM MATER, MOTHER.` · `THE COUPLE ARE THE MINISTERS.` · `NOT TWO, BUT ONE FLESH.` · `THIS IS A GREAT SACRAMENT.` · then, large: `TWO MINISTERS, ONE PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember a married couple. Settle, and breathe. Think of two people you know who have been together a long time. Your grandparents, your parents, neighbors, friends. Picture them on an ordinary day: one making coffee, the other reading out the news. Think of what it's taken them to keep that promise. The bad years, the sick years, the funny ones. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, just be glad for them. The bell holds the time.
Matrimony. From the Latin for mother. The sacrament two people give each other, with their own promise. Today's word.

Your line: two ministers, one promise. That's the seven sacraments: baptism, confirmation, Eucharist, reconciliation, anointing, orders, matrimony. Today, tell a couple you know what you admire in them. Day one hundred thirty-two.

133.title: The examination of conscience
133.hook: a slow look back using the commandments or the beatitudes
133.howItsDone: Before confession, and often each night, Catholics examine their conscience with a printed guide based on the Ten Commandments, the Beatitudes or the works of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, matrimony, the sacrament a couple give each other. Your line was two ministers, one promise. Did you tell a couple what you admire? Day one hundred thirty-three.

Eleven at night, lights off, and the day starts replaying. That thing you said at lunch. The email you sent too fast. The tape runs again and again, and it isn't kind. Catholics keep an old practice that does the same review on purpose, slowly, with a guide, and in a different voice: not a prosecutor, more like a good doctor. Honest about what's wrong, and on your side. It has a name, and this week we'll follow it all the way into the confessional. Today's word: conscience.
screen: `REPLAYING THE DAY AT NIGHT.` → `NOT A PROSECUTOR.` → `A GOOD DOCTOR.`

segments.voice: Conscience comes from Latin, conscientia: knowing with. Knowing something together with yourself, the part of you that sees what you did and knows what it meant. The Catholic Church teaches that conscience is where a person is alone with God, a kind of inner sanctuary where God's voice can be heard, and that everyone is bound to follow a well-formed conscience. John Henry Newman, the English convert and cardinal, put it memorably in 1875: "Conscience is the aboriginal Vicar of Christ." Aboriginal meaning first, original: before any pope or priest, there's that voice within. An examination of conscience is the practice of listening to it on purpose. Before confession, Catholics often go slowly through a guide. A common one uses the Ten Commandments: have I put anything in God's place? Have I been honest? Have I treated my parents with respect? Another uses the Beatitudes: have I been merciful? Have I made peace, or stirred things up? Some use the works of mercy. Some do a short version every night. Today's carry holds the center of it. An examination is not a trial where you're the defendant. Catholic spiritual writers warn against scrupulosity, a harsh, anxious picking at yourself that never finds rest. The point of looking is to see clearly enough to be healed. You look honestly, because you can't ask forgiveness for what you won't admit. And you look without harshness, because the one you're looking with, Catholics believe, is merciful. Tomorrow we walk through the door of the confessional.
screen: `CONSCIENTIA: KNOWING WITH.` · `THE ABORIGINAL VICAR OF CHRIST.` · `COMMANDMENTS, BEATITUDES, MERCY.` · `NOT A TRIAL. NOT SCRUPLES.` · then, large: `LOOK HONESTLY, NOT HARSHLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a slow look back. Settle, and breathe. Go back through the last day, like a film, from waking up until now. Where were you patient? Where were you short with someone? Where were you honest? Where did you shade the truth? Notice, don't judge. If something stands out, just name it to yourself, plainly. Then name one thing you did well, because that belongs in the look back too. If you pray, you can hand both to God. The bell holds the time.
Conscience. From the Latin for knowing with. The inner voice Catholics believe is where a person meets God, and a slow, honest look back by its light. Today's word.

Your line: look honestly, not harshly. This week: confirmation, the Eucharist, reconciliation, anointing, ordination, matrimony, and conscience. Tonight, before sleep, give the day one gentle look back. Day one hundred thirty-three.
